chunks: Power planes and shapes vs traces. The question: What is a power plane/shapes? Why are they preferred over traces?
A power plane is a whole layer of the board that is solid copper on one net, such as ground or 3. 3 volts.
A shape, or pour, is the same idea over just part of a layer that also holds traces. Both beat a thin trace for carrying power.
Current spreads out across the sheet in two dimensions, so the resistance is much lower, the inductance is lower, and heat spreads too.
Picture a river and a garden hose carrying the same flow. The hose forces all the water through one narrow tube.
The river lets it spread across a wide bed, so there is far less friction. A plane is the river.
The catch is that anything blocking the riverbed, such as a long slot cut across it, forces the flow to detour.
The trace forces all current through one narrow ribbon.
The plane lets current fan out along many parallel paths, so most of the resistance sits right next to the two vias and the middle contributes very little.
Sheet resistance: the resistance of one square of copper, about 0. 48 milliohms for 1 oz copper ("High-current layout rules of thumb").
Plane: a layer of mostly solid copper on one net. Shape (pour, polygon): a copper area on a routing layer.
Return current: the current's path back to its source, which at high frequency runs directly under the signal ("Ground plane pros and cons").
Split or slot: a gap in a plane that forces return current to detour.
A 1 mm wide trace that is 25 mm long is 25 squares. At 0. 48 milliohms per square, that is 12 milliohms. Now feed the same current into a plane through a 0.
5 mm radius via and collect it 25 mm away. The resistance is 0. 48 over 2 pi log (25 over 0. 5) about 0. 30 milliohms, about 40 times lower, because the current fans out.
That is the whole idea.
"A power plane is a full layer of copper on one net; a shape or pour is a copper area on a layer shared with routing.
They beat traces because current spreads in two dimensions, so resistance only grows with the log of distance instead of linearly, giving much less drop and heating.
A plane close to its return also has very low inductance and some built-in capacitance, and it spreads heat.
The catches are splits that break return paths and big shapes on noisy or sensitive nodes."
